title: Manifest schema: types, YAML parsing, KnownFields validation
description:
Package: internal/manifest

Types (locked by spec): Tool, Target, Verify, VersionCheck. Tool.Install is
map[string]Target keyed by GOOS. Validation uses yaml.Decoder.KnownFields(true)
so a typo field fails loudly rather than being silently dropped.

CONTRACT:
- Name must be lowercase kebab-case and non-empty
- Description required
- verify: null is VALID (presence-only check). verify: null + empty provides
  = validation error (nothing would be checked)
- verify.version without verify.command = validation error
- Unknown strategy = error listing valid set. NEVER default to github-release
- Self-referential dependency = error

Per-strategy required/rejected field matrix (locked in spec):
  github-release: needs repository+asset+sha256; rejects manager/package/go_package/npm_package/cargo_name
  package+brew:   needs manager:brew+package; rejects repository/asset/sha256
  package+apt:    needs manager:apt+package; same rejections
  go:             needs go_package; rejects manager/package/repository/asset/sha256
  npm:            needs npm_package; same rejections as go
  cargo:          needs cargo_name; same rejections as go

Cross-cutting:
- asset keys and sha256 keys must cover EXACTLY the same arch set
- every key must be a valid Go arch (arm64/amd64). x86_64 in an asset key is an
  ERROR naming the offending key -- never a silent fallback
- manager other than brew/apt = error

Tests (contract, not source-grep):
- missing required field -> error naming that exact field
- unknown field (typo) -> error
- verify: null with provides -> VALID
- verify: null without provides -> error
- verify.version without verify.command -> error
- github-release missing sha256[amd64] while asset[amd64] present -> error
- asset/sha256 arch-set mismatch -> error
- asset key 'x86_64' -> error naming the key
- unknown strategy 'gihub-release' -> error listing valid set
- unknown manager 'port' -> error
- round trip: parse -> marshal -> parse yields equal Tool

This is a PURE package. No filesystem access beyond reading the manifest path.
No imports of platform, resolver, or installer.
close_reason: manifest package rewritten to locked spec: Tool/Target/Verify/VersionCheck, KnownFields(true), closed strategy matrix, Go-arch vocabulary, removal hints. 52 test assertions, race-clean.

title: Platform detection: OS, arch, package manager
description:
Package: internal/platform

Types: Host{OS, Arch, Manager, Prefix}. Functions: Current(), (h) Key(),
(h) Supports(tool), (h) Has(bin).

ARCH VOCABULARY (critical -- three vocabularies collide here):
  install: map key  = darwin|linux   (runtime.GOOS)
  Host.Arch        = arm64|amd64     (runtime.GOARCH, Go naming)
  uname -m         = arm64|x86_64    (system, only when shelling out)

AES uses Go naming EVERYWHERE. Host.Arch is runtime.GOARCH verbatim -- no
translation layer exists inside AES. Provide unameArchToGo() for the ONE place
that shells out to uname (install.sh and any uname invocation).

Homebrew prefix detection order: /opt/homebrew/bin/brew (Apple Silicon),
then /usr/local/bin/brew (Intel), then brew on PATH. Return the prefix DIR.

Manager detection: 'brew' only if a usable brew found. On Linux, 'apt' when
apt-get is present. PRESENCE CHECK ONLY -- never run apt-get to 'verify', that
would be a side effect.

Tests:
- Key() maps each GOOS constant correctly -- TABLE TEST over darwin/linux,
  never asserting the current host
- Supports() with a darwin-only tool on linux host -> false (construct Host
  explicitly rather than reading Current(), so the test is host-independent)
- Supports() tool with no install entry for this platform -> false
- Has("") -> false (callers pass user input; empty must be safe)
- Has("sh") -> true (near-universal, safe cross-platform)
- unameArchToGo: x86_64->amd64, aarch64->arm64, amd64->amd64, arm64->arm64
- Homebrew prefix: each candidate dir tested via t.TempDir, assert the right
  one wins regardless of what the real machine has

Host must be comparable and JSON-serializable: it is embedded by pointer in
resolver.Action.
close_reason: internal/platform landed: Host{OS,Arch,Manager,Prefix} comparable+JSON-serializable, Current/Key/Supports/Target/Has/Path, unameArchToGo translation table, brew prefix detection split for testability. 32 assertions, host-independent table tests, race-clean.

title: Verifier: presence, version extraction, status classification
description:
Package: internal/verifier

Types: Status (ok|missing|stale), Result{Tool,Status,Version,Path}.
func Verify(t *manifest.Tool) Result -- returns NO error for a normal outcome.
A missing tool is StatusMissing, not an error. An error would mean 'could not
determine', which is a different thing and the signature should probably grow
a separate method later.

VERSION EXTRACTION -- every tool prints differently, one lenient parser:
  ripgrep 14.1.1                      -> 14.1.1
  fzf 0.54.0 (brew)                   -> 0.54.0
  git version 2.44.0                  -> 2.44.0
  go version go1.24.0 darwin/arm64    -> 1.24.0   (strip the 'v'/'go' prefix)
  jq-1.7.1                            -> 1.7.1
  claude 1.0.283 (Claude Code)        -> 1.0.283
  tmux 3.4                            -> 3.4
  zoxide 0.9.4                        -> 0.9.4

Algorithm:
1. First line of output, trimmed
2. First \d+(\.\d+)* run in the line, optional leading 'v' stripped
3. Compare as DOTTED INTEGERS not semver: missing components are zero
   (14.1 == 14.1.0), so min:'14.0' matches 14.1.1

CRITICAL: no digits -> no version. Return Version:'' with StatusOK when only
presence was being checked. NEVER guess, NEVER fabricate a number.

Comparison: StatusStale when extracted < min, StatusOK when >= min. A tool
NEWER than the minimum is fine -- AES never downgrades.

Verify NEVER reads state.json. Verify is the ground truth; state is a cache.

Tests (table-driven, all versions above as cases):
- each real-world version string -> expected extraction
- '14.1' vs min '14.1.0' -> OK (dotted-integer equality, NOT semver inequality)
- '14.0.9' vs min '14.1' -> Stale
- '15.0' vs min '14.9' -> OK (newer is fine, no downgrade)
- no digits in output -> Version empty, Status stays OK
- empty output -> same as no digits
- multiline output -> only the FIRST line is parsed
- command on PATH -> OK; absent -> Missing
- verify: null + provides -> presence-only check works
- a provides entry missing while command resolves -> detected (Missing)

Pure package: no writes, no state access. Only exec.LookPath + running the
version command with a short timeout.
notes: [2026-09-26 17:27:52 UTC] VioletOtter claimed. Building on MagentaHawk's 3g5. Verifier is platform-INDEPENDENT by construction (Verify/Provides live on Tool, install strategy on per-GOOS Target) - will confirm.
close_reason: VioletOtter: internal/verifier implemented. Lenient first-digit-run version parser (8 real-world formats), dotted-integer comparison (14.1==14.1.0), no fabrication when no digits. All binaries (verify.command + provides) must resolve. 14 tests, -race clean, 98.1% coverage. Mutation-verified: dropping provides detection fails 3 tests; semver-instead-of-dotted-int fails the equality case. Verify takes no Host - see agent mail rationale.

title: State store: atomic write, corruption detection, version guard
description:
Package: internal/state

Types: File{Version, Installed map[string]Installed},
Installed{Strategy, Privileged, Version, InstalledAt}. const Version = 1.

THREE RULES (these are invariants I4/I5/I9, do not weaken them):
1. State is written ONLY after verify passes. Failure NEVER writes.
2. State is a CACHE. Verify is ground truth; doctor compares the two and
   reports drift. A state file that says 'installed' while the binary is gone
   is exactly what doctor exists to catch.
3. A CORRUPT state file is an ERROR, never an empty state. Treating corruption
   as 'nothing installed' causes a reinstall storm -- the tool would reinstall
   40 things because one JSON file got truncated.

ATOMIC WRITE: temp file in the SAME directory + os.Rename. A crash mid-write
must never leave corrupt JSON. A .tmp file must not survive a successful save.

PERMISSIONS: dir 0700, file 0600. This is security-relevant -- state records
what is installed on a developer machine.

VERSION GUARD: if the on-disk Version is HIGHER than const Version, return a
clear error naming both versions. DO NOT silently discard the user's data.

Tests:
- MISSING file -> empty state, NO error (first run must not crash)
- CORRUPT json -> error, and specifically NOT an empty state (assert this
  directly: the returned state must be non-empty OR the error non-nil)
- save -> load round trip preserves all entries
- atomic: after a successful Save, no .tmp file remains in the dir
- atomic: a Save interrupted mid-write leaves the ORIGINAL file intact and
  parseable (simulate by making the target unwritable, or by injecting a
  failure -- do not merely assert the happy path)
- version higher than const -> error naming the version, original bytes intact
- permissions: dir 0700, file 0600 (skip on non-unix)
- concurrent Save from two goroutines -> file always parses (run with -race)

No dependencies on manifest, resolver, or installer. This package is a pure
keyed store over a file path.
notes: [2026-09-26 17:19:50 UTC] VioletOtter claimed 2026-09-27. internal/state/ reserved. Starting: atomic write + corruption detection + version guard.
close_reason: VioletOtter: internal/state implemented. Atomic write (temp+fsync+rename), corruption=ErrCorrupt never empty state (I9), version guard names both versions, 0700/0600. 12 tests, -race clean, 84% coverage. Mutation-verified: reverting the corruption guard fails 4 subtests.

title: Catalog: load tool.yaml files, index by name/category/tag
description:
Package: internal/catalog

Loads every tool.yaml under tools/<category>/<name>/tool.yaml. Note the
directory is a convenience for humans; Category is a FIELD in the YAML and is
the source of truth. Never read the category from the path.

Indexes needed by the resolver:
  byName map[string]*manifest.Tool
  byCategory map[string][]*manifest.Tool
  byTag map[string][]*manifest.Tool

Also: Default() returns every tool with default:true, in deterministic order.

ERROR BEHAVIOUR: loading is all-or-nothing. If ANY tool.yaml fails validation,
load returns an error naming that file and the reason. Do NOT silently skip a
broken file -- a typo'd manifest that vanishes produces a setup that quietly
omits a tool the user expected.

Duplicate tool names across directories is an error, not last-wins.

Tests:
- load a t.TempDir() catalog with 3 valid tools -> all present in byName
- one invalid tool -> error names the FILE (not just the field)
- duplicate name in two dirs -> error
- byCategory/byTag indexes resolve correctly
- Default() returns only default:true tools, sorted by name
- empty catalog dir -> empty indexes, NO error
- load order is deterministic: two loads of the same dir produce identical
  key ordering (sort explicitly, do not rely on map iteration)

Depends on manifest (types + validation).
close_reason: VioletOtter: internal/catalog implemented. All-or-nothing load naming the file, ErrDuplicateTool over last-wins, byName/byCategory/byTag/Default/Tested indexes, category from the YAML field never the path, explicit sort so no walk-order leaks. 15 tests, -race clean, 93.7% cov. Mutation-verified: skipping broken manifests fails 4 subtests; last-wins duplicate handling fails 1.

title: Resolver: dependency DAG, cycle detection, deterministic Actions
description:
Package: internal/resolver

Types: Operation (install|upgrade), Action{Tool, Strategy, Operation, Host
*platform.Host, RequiresPrivilege, Reason}, Request{Profile, Only, Exclude}.
func Resolve(c *catalog.Catalog, req Request, h *platform.Host) ([]Action, error)

PIPELINE, always in this order:
  profile -> only/exclude -> dependency closure -> platform filter -> Actions

DEPENDENCY BEATS SELECTION. '--only claude' still pulls claude's deps.
Excluding a required dep is an ERROR naming who needs it:
  'node is required by claude' -- never silently break the graph.

ACTION SEMANTICS (locked in spec):
- Identity = Tool + Strategy + Operation. A diamond dependency yields ONE
  action, not two.
- Ordering is TOPOLOGICAL (deps first), ties broken by tool NAME. Identical
  input yields byte-identical output.
- Deduplication happens BEFORE ordering, keyed on identity.
- Reason is a plain diagnostic string: 'default' | 'dependency:git' |
  'only:claude'. Never parsed, never an enum -- doctor displays it, nothing
  consumes it programmatically.
- RequiresPrivilege is DERIVED from (Strategy, Manager) -- NEVER read from
  YAML. github-release->false, package+brew->false, package+apt->TRUE,
  go/npm/cargo->false.
- Host is a POINTER, shared across all actions in one resolution. Action is a
  RESOLVED SNAPSHOT, not an execution context: the installer consumes this
  Host and does NOT re-resolve. If reality differs at execution time that is
  drift, and drift is doctor's job. This keeps Resolve pure and testable
  without touching the filesystem.
- No []string slices on Action, so JSON serialization is deterministic.

DAG in dag.go: cycle detection + topological sort. A cycle must ERROR, never
hang, never return partial results.

Tests:
- A->B->A cycle -> cycle error, NEVER hangs (guard the test with a timeout)
- self-dependency -> cycle error
- diamond A->B,A->C,B->D,C->D -> D appears exactly once
- '--only claude' where claude needs git -> actions include git
- '--exclude node' while claude needs node -> error naming the requirement
- '--exclude' of a tool nothing needs -> silently excluded, no error
- same input twice -> byte-identical Actions (compare the serialized form)
- profile resolution -> exactly the default:true tools
- unsupported-platform tool in the profile -> EXCLUDED from actions, and the
  exclusion is NOT an error
- tool with no install entry for this GOOS -> excluded, not an error
- Reason populated correctly on the default/dependency/only paths
- topological order: every action's deps appear BEFORE it (assert across the
  whole slice, not pairwise spot checks)
- the returned Action list is non-nil even when empty (so callers can range
  over it without a nil check)

Depends on manifest, catalog, platform.
notes: [2026-09-26 17:33:14 UTC] VioletOtter claimed. sqw closed. Building DAG in dag.go + deterministic Actions.
close_reason: VioletOtter: internal/resolver implemented. dag.go does Kahn topo sort with name tie-break + cycle path reporting (a->b->a); resolver.go does selection->exclusion->closure->cycle->platform filter->Actions. RequiresPrivilege derived from (Strategy,Manager). 18 tests, -race clean, 91.6% cov. Mutation-verified: partial-order-on-cycle fails 4, dropping the tie-break fails 4, ignoring exclusions fails 1, package+brew privilege fails 1.

title: Exec: run commands with timeout, output capture, sudo gate
description:
Package: internal/exec

The safety gate lives HERE, structurally, not as a comment.

func Run(ctx, cmd string, opts Options) (Result, error)
Result{Stdout, Stderr, ExitCode, Duration}. Options{Dir, Timeout, Stdin, Env}.

SUDO GATE (the single most important invariant here, I10/I14):
Scan the command for 'sudo' BEFORE running. If present, return
PrivilegeError{Command, NonInteractive} and DO NOT EXECUTE.

The core NEVER silently escalates. The privilege MODEL, specified in the
comprehensive doc, is:
  interactive:     print the command, confirm with the user, then run
  non-interactive: try 'sudo -n' (CI NOPASSWD or cached credential);
                   on failure print the command and return the error --
                   NEVER block waiting for a password
The distinction between 'we will not sudo' and 'we will sudo after asking'
lives in the installer, which calls this package. This package's job is to
refuse to run a sudo command that was handed to it directly.

EXECUTION: cmd is a SHELL COMMAND STRING (manifest run: fields are things like
'brew install ripgrep'). Use sh -c on unix. Document this in the package doc.
Enforce timeouts via context.WithTimeout + exec.CommandContext -- a hung
apt-get must not hang AES forever. Default 10min for install, 5s for verify.

OUTPUT: capture stdout and stderr SEPARATELY. On non-zero exit return BOTH
the error and the Result, so the caller can show the user what went wrong. A
failed install that swallows brew's output is useless. Cap each stream at
1 MiB with a visible truncation marker -- a runaway command must not exhaust
memory.

A timeout must SAY SO: 'timed out after 10m' is actionable, a generic
'signal: killed' is not.

Tests (must pass on macOS AND linux CI):
- SUDO REFUSAL: Run(ctx, 'sudo touch /tmp/aes-should-not-exist-N') returns
  PrivilegeError AND the file does not exist afterwards. Assert the SIDE
  EFFECT is absent -- that is the real contract, not the error value.
- sudo as a substring anywhere in the command -> still refused
- 'echo hello' -> Stdout contains hello, ExitCode 0
- non-zero exit (e.g. 'exit 3') -> error returned AND Result.ExitCode==3
  AND stderr populated (proves output is not swallowed on failure)
- timeout: a command outliving a 200ms timeout returns an error whose text
  mentions the timeout, not a generic kill signal
- output cap: 'yes' piped to 'head' producing more than the cap is truncated
  with a visible marker (portable across mac/linux)
- empty command -> error, no execution
- Env nil -> inherits os.Environ()
- Stdin is forwarded (echo a known string through it)

No dependency on manifest, resolver, or installer.
notes: [2026-09-26 17:19:50 UTC] VioletOtter claimed 2026-09-27 (queued after fvu). internal/exec/ reserved. Scope: sudo gate lives structurally in Run(), not in a comment.
close_reason: VioletOtter: internal/exec implemented. Sudo gate is structural (regex check before exec), refuses without spawning. Separate stdout/stderr, 1MiB cap with visible marker, timeouts named not 'signal: killed', Result returned alongside errors. 15 tests, -race clean, 98% coverage. Mutation-verified: deleting the gate fails 7 subtests incl. the side-effect assertion.

title: Installer registry + github-release strategy with sha256 gate
description:
Packages: internal/installer (+ github_release.go)

type Installer interface { Install(ctx, Action) error }
registry: map strategy -> Installer. RESOLUTION IS BY STRATEGY, NEVER
switch tool.Name. Invariant I1 -- this is what lets the tool count grow from
10 to 300 without touching core.

NewRegistry() registers the implemented strategies. An unknown strategy name
returns an error listing the valid set -- never a silent default.

GITHUB-RELEASE STRATEGY (the primary path):
  1. resolve the asset for GOOS+GOARCH from the action's Target.Asset
  2. download to a temp file
  3. verify sha256 against Target.SHA256[arch]
  4. MISMATCH -> abort immediately. NEVER extract a file that failed
     verification. This is the single most important safety property.
  5. extract (tar.gz) into ~/.aes/bin
  6. chmod +x
  7. clean up the temp file even on failure

The download URL derives from Repository + asset name against the GitHub
releases download endpoint. SUPPORT A VERSION/TAG FIELD so assets are
pinned. An unpinned 'latest' is a supply-chain risk: the binary changes under
you with no record.

ARCH RULE: asset and sha256 keys are GO ARCH (arm64/amd64), never x86_64. The
key for the current host MUST be present; a missing key errors naming the
arch. NEVER fall back to amd64 or to the first available key.

ARCHIVE SAFETY: before extracting, reject any entry containing a path
traversal component ('..') or an absolute path. An archive that can write
outside the destination is a code-execution vector, not a cosmetic issue.

Tests:
- WRONG SHA256 -> abort, and assert ~/.aes/bin received NO FILE. The absence
  of the file is the contract; the error message is not.
- correct sha256 -> binary present, executable bit set
- asset key missing for the current arch -> error naming the arch
- sha256 key missing while asset key present -> error naming the arch
- network failure -> clean error, no partial file
- temp file cleaned up on BOTH success and failure paths
- tarball with a ../ entry -> rejected, nothing extracted outside destination
- tarball with an absolute-path entry -> rejected
- unknown strategy -> error listing the valid set
- registry resolves each known strategy to a distinct non-nil Installer
- the temp file and any partially-extracted content are cleaned up when
  verification fails (not just when download fails)

Depends on manifest, platform, exec.
close_reason: internal/installer landed: registry resolves by strategy (I1, unknown strategy errors naming valid set, never defaults to github-release), github-release strategy with download->verify->extract ordering, per-arch asset/sha256 lookup with no fallback, archive traversal/absolute-path rejection, staging cleanup on every path. 24 assertions; checksum-gate mutation-verified.

title: Package strategy (brew/apt) with the privilege model
description:
Package: internal/installer/package.go

Implements the two package-manager installers and, critically, the PRIVILEGE
MODEL that the spec locks in.

BREW:  brew install <package>
       No privilege needed. Runs directly, no prompt.

APT:   Requires privilege. The model:
         interactive:     PRINT the command, ask for confirmation, then run
         non-interactive: try 'sudo -n' (CI NOPASSWD or cached credential)
                          -> success: run
                          -> failure: PRINT the command, return
                             PrivilegeError, exit code 5. NEVER block
                             waiting for a password.

RATIONALE (do not 'simplify' this away): the risk in sudo is not sudo, it is
WHO CHOSE THE COMMAND. Silent sudo + a malicious tool.yaml = a bad actor gets
your password. sudo that PRINTS AND ASKS means you see what is about to run.
The rule is: never run silently -- but never refuse outright. Refusing
outright would break the North Star (aes setup is ONE command that runs to
completion on a normal machine).

THREE ENFORCEABLE TERMS, each testable:
1. sudo never runs unasked. exec.Command('sudo', ...) executes only after the
   command is printed and, when interactive, confirmed.
2. --non-interactive uses sudo -n. Never blocks on a password prompt.
3. A required manual step returns exit code 5 and does NOT mark state done.

HOW TO TEST WITHOUT ACTUALLY SUDOING: the test harness must be able to inject
a fake runner. Design PackageInstaller with a function field (or interface)
for command execution so tests substitute a recorder. Then assert on the
RECORDED invocations:
- interactive, no confirmation input -> runner NOT called with sudo
- interactive, confirmation given -> runner called with the exact command
- non-interactive, sudo -n succeeds -> runner called
- non-interactive, sudo -n fails -> error, exit 5, no retry loop, no hang
- brew -> runner called with 'brew install <pkg>', never with sudo

The exit code 5 mapping lives in the CLI layer, not here -- this package
returns PrivilegeError and the CLI maps it.

Depends on manifest, exec.
close_reason: internal/installer/package.go landed: brew runs unprivileged with no prompt; apt implements the full privilege model (print-then-confirm interactive, sudo -n non-interactive, never blocks, PrivilegeError for CLI exit-code-5 mapping). Two-runner split keeps the sudo capability visible in the type. 15 assertions; confirmation gate and retry-loop both mutation-verified.

title: envgen: deterministic env.sh with ownership marker
description:
Package: internal/envgen

func Generate(tools, home) ([]byte, error)
func Write(path, tools, home) error   -- ATOMIC

THE CONTEXT THAT SHAPES THIS: the user's shell broke silently in Sept 2026.
Their old tool made .zshrc delegate to a config dir behind 'if [[ -f ]]' with
no else branch. The dir was deleted, the guard went false, and the shell came
up looking NORMAL with no theme, no plugins, no prompt config. Nobody noticed
for days. This package is the fix; do not regress it.

PATH IS NOT JUST ~/.aes/bin. Different strategies install to different
places, and env.sh is what makes them reachable:
  github-release -> ~/.aes/bin        (aes always owns this)
  go              -> ~/go/bin
  npm             -> the user npm global prefix
  cargo           -> ~/.cargo/bin
  uv              -> ~/.local/bin
  brew/apt        -> already on PATH via the package manager; contribute
                     nothing
So Generate() must include, for each INSTALLED tool, that strategy's
destination directory -- deduplicated across tools, in deterministic order.
A user who installs a go-based tool and never sources env.sh has a tool that
installed successfully and is not runnable. That is a broken setup wearing a
success message.

RULES:
- Header is the OWNERSHIP MARKER, unmistakable:
    # Generated by aes -- DO NOT EDIT BY HAND
    # Regenerate with: aes env --write
  Refuse to overwrite a file lacking it (ErrNotGenerated). A hand-written
  env.sh is the user's work, not ours to clobber.
- DETERMINISTIC: same input -> byte-identical output. No timestamp in the
  body. Sort every directory. Two runs must diff clean.
- IDEMPOTENT sourcing: guard each PATH append with a 'case $PATH' check.
- Quote values for shell: a value containing quote, dollar, or newline must
  not break the file. Single-quote escaping with the standard '\\'' form.
- Dedupe: two tools setting the same var -> exactly one export, winner by
  sorted-name order, never last-write-wins by map order.
- Atomic write: temp file in the same dir + rename. A half-written env.sh
  breaks the user's shell on next login -- the worst possible failure here.
- File mode 0644.
- NEVER write ~/.zshrc or any shell rc. That is --link-shell's job, a
  separate explicit opt-in. This package generates the env file and nothing
  else.

Tests:
- byte-identical output for the same input across two calls with DIFFERENT
  tool orderings -- determinism, easy to break by iterating a map
- a go-strategy tool contributes ~/go/bin; a cargo tool contributes
  ~/.cargo/bin; a brew tool contributes NOTHING
- a tool installed in two strategies appears once
- header contains 'DO NOT EDIT' and the regeneration command
- shell quoting: a value of 'it'"'"'s $HOME "x"' round-trips through a
  REAL shell (execute sh -c 'source file; echo $VAR') -- stronger than a
  string comparison
- a newline in a value does not break the generated file
- dedupe: two tools setting FOO -> exactly one export, deterministic winner
- REFUSAL: pre-existing file without the header -> error AND the file is
  byte-identical afterwards (prove no clobber)
- atomic: existing generated file + new content -> updated, no .tmp left
- PATH guard: sourcing twice is a no-op

Depends on manifest, platform, and the installer package (for the
strategy-to-destination mapping).
close_reason: internal/envgen landed: deterministic env.sh (no timestamp, everything sorted), ownership-marker refusal that leaves a hand-written file byte-identical, atomic same-dir temp+rename at mode 0644, guarded PATH appends, shell quoting that round-trips through a real sh. 14 assertions incl. two real-shell tests; 3 mutations (ownership, sort, dedupe) all caught.

title: CLI framework: command tree, flag contract, exit code mapping
description:
Packages: internal/cli/root.go, cmd/aes/main.go

Command tree: aes setup | list | verify | doctor | env  (MVP)
Bare 'aes' is reserved for the TUI later; for now it prints help.

EXIT CODE CONTRACT (locked in spec; this is how an agent parses us):
  0  all resolved actions verified
  1  generic failure
  2  invalid usage / bad flags
  3  catalog or manifest invalid
  4  unsupported platform
  5  NEEDS A MANUAL PRIVILEGED STEP  <- distinct so an agent can tell
     'you must do something' from 'it broke'
  6  verification failed after install

Central mapping lives in ONE function so no command invents its own codes.

FLAG SEMANTICS -- --yes and --non-interactive are NOT synonyms and neither
implies the other:
  --yes             = 'I am at a terminal, do not ask me'
                     REQUIRES a TTY. Piping it without one is a USAGE ERROR
                     (exit 2), never a silent downgrade -- that combination
                     is exactly how a CI job hangs on a prompt nobody sees.
  --non-interactive = 'there is nobody to ask'. Every confirmation resolves
                     automatically: sudo -n first, else skip + print + exit 5.
                     Never blocks on stdin.
  both              = legal, --non-interactive wins, but pointless
  --dry-run         = orthogonal. Resolves, prints actions, exits 0, mutates
                     NOTHING, regardless of the other flags.
  --json            = machine-parseable; NO human text mixed into stdout

--force semantics (it is NOT 'delete everything and reinstall'):
  StatusMissing + no state    -> install
  StatusStale                 -> install
  DRIFTED (state says installed, verify says missing) -> without --force:
     report, exit 6.  With --force: reinstall.
  checksum mismatch on prior install -> without: report, exit 6.
     With --force: reinstall after the fix.
--force NEVER widens the resolved set. An excluded tool stays excluded.

Tests:
- each command returns the documented exit code for its failure mode
- PrivilegeError -> exit 5 specifically
- manifest validation error -> exit 3
- unsupported platform -> exit 4
- 'aes setup --yes' with stdin not a TTY -> exit 2 with a clear message
- --non-interactive with no stdin -> never blocks (test with a timeout guard)
- --json output parses as JSON and contains no human prose
- unknown flag -> exit 2 with usage

Depends on manifest, catalog, resolver, platform, verifier, state, envgen,
installer (for exit 5 mapping).

title: aes setup orchestration: the North Star path
description:
Package: internal/cli/setup.go

THE NORTH STAR. ONE COMMAND takes a machine from 'nothing' to 'complete,
verified AI coding environment', exiting 0 only when done.

PIPELINE, always in this order:
  1. detect host
  2. load profile
  3. resolve Actions
  4. verify CURRENT state (for every resolved tool, BEFORE installing)
  5. install what is missing
  6. verify AGAIN  <-- this gates the state write
  7. write state (only tools that passed step 6)
  8. generate env
  9. summary

IDEMPOTENCY IS A HARD REQUIREMENT: 'aes setup' dying at tool 27 and re-run
must not reinstall 1-26. This falls out of step 4 -- verify current state
first, and a tool already OK is not an install candidate. Do NOT rely on
state.json to decide this; VERIFY decides it. State is a cache. This is
exactly the resume behaviour the ACFS comparison identified as worth having.

RESUME: a re-run continues from whatever is already correct. Never assume a
clean machine.

FAILURE CONTAINMENT: one tool failing does NOT abort the whole run. Continue
with the remaining tools, collect failures, and exit 6 at the end with a full
report. Aborting on the first failure wastes the work already done and
destroys the resume property. Exceptions that DO abort immediately: catalog
failure (nothing can proceed) and manifest validation failure (exit 3).

ORDER OF OPERATIONS: state is written ONLY for tools that passed step 6. A
tool that installed but failed verification is reported, exits 6, and gets NO
state entry. A half-written state is worse than none.

SUMMARY must state plainly: installed / already present / skipped / failed
counts, and where env.sh landed. If a manual privileged step is needed, print
the exact command and exit 5. Do NOT claim success when something needs a
human.

--dry-run stops after step 4 and prints the Actions. Mutates nothing.

Tests (the 10 MVP assertions from the spec):
 1. list shows status derived from VERIFY, not from state
 2. setup --dry-run prints actions and changes no file (snapshot the whole
    ~/.aes tree before/after, not just state.json)
 3. install runs the resolved strategy (inject a recording installer)
 4. verify pass -> state written
 5. re-run is idempotent: second run calls the installer ZERO times
 6. corrupt state -> error, NOT treated as 'nothing installed'
 7. corrupt manifest -> exit 3, installer NEVER called
 8. unsupported-platform tool -> skipped, not an error, not installed
 9. privilege-requiring strategy -> command printed BEFORE any sudo attempt;
    with no confirmation, sudo never runs
10. install succeeds but verification fails -> exit 6, state NOT written for
    that tool, summary reports it as failed
11. one tool fails but others still install (failure containment)
12. exit 5 when a privileged manual step is required

Depends on manifest, catalog, resolver, platform, verifier, state, envgen,
installer, profile.

title: list, verify, doctor, env commands
description:
Package: internal/cli/{list,verify,doctor,env}.go

LIST:  aes list [--json]
  Status comes from VERIFY, never from state. That distinction is the whole
  point -- a tool whose state says 'installed' but whose binary is gone must
  show as missing here.
  Columns: name, category, status (ok/missing/stale), version, path.
  Tests: a tool with a faked-missing binary shows missing even though state
  claims installed; --json parses and contains no prose.

VERIFY: aes verify [tool...] [--json]
  Tool-level check, does not mutate. Equivalent to list but scoped and with
  a non-zero exit when anything is not ok (so CI can use it as a gate).
  Tests: specific tool names verified; no args verifies the whole catalog;
  a stale tool yields a distinct non-zero exit from a missing one.

DOCTOR: aes doctor [--json]
  Environment-wide health, and its special job is DRIFT DETECTION (I5):
  compare state.json against Verify and report every disagreement:
    - state says installed, verify says missing  -> DRIFTED
    - state says installed, verify says stale    -> outdated
    - state absent, verify says ok               -> unmanaged (present but
      AES does not track it -- informational, not an error)
  Also check: PATH contains ~/.aes/bin, the shell rc sources env.sh if
  --link-shell was used, untested tools in the default profile (I15 warning),
  package manager availability for tools that need one.
  CRITICAL: doctor REPORTS, it does not fix. There is no --fix in the MVP.
  A self-fixing doctor makes changes the user cannot see.
  Tests: drift detected for each of the three cases above; doctor makes NO
  filesystem changes (directory snapshot before/after).

ENV: aes env [--write] [--link-shell]
  Default prints the content. --write generates ~/.aes/env.sh atomically
  (delegates to envgen). --link-shell is a SEPARATE explicit opt-in that
  appends a delimited block to the shell rc, and only then:
    1. detect the shell and its rc file
    2. back up the rc file FIRST
    3. check for an existing aes block (idempotent -- do not append twice)
    4. append:
         # >>> aes env >>>
         [ -f "$HOME/.aes/env.sh" ] && source "$HOME/.aes/env.sh"
         # <<< aes env <<<
    5. offer restore from the backup
  AES manages ONLY its own delimited block, never rewrites the whole rc.
  Tests: --link-shell on an rc already containing the block -> no duplicate;
  backup created before modification; the rc is otherwise byte-identical
  outside the block; a second run is a no-op.

Depends on manifest, catalog, resolver, platform, verifier, state, envgen.
close_reason: list/verify/doctor/env landed in internal/cli. Status comes from verify not state (drift visible); verify exits 6 as a CI gate; doctor reports drift/outdated/unmanaged and makes NO filesystem changes (asserted by tree snapshot); env --write is atomic and --link-shell backs up the rc first, manages only its delimited block, and is idempotent. All 45 CLI assertions green under -race.

title: Stage 0 bootstrap: build, install.sh, GitHub Release
description:
Tier 0. This is the REAL entry point -- without it, every later stage is
code on paper. Build it early.

Files: install.sh, scripts/build.sh, .github/workflows/release.yml

install.sh does EXACTLY FIVE THINGS and nothing else:
  1. detect OS + arch
  2. download the binary from GitHub Releases
  3. verify sha256
  4. place it at ~/.aes/bin/aes
  5. run 'aes --version'

It installs NO TOOLS. Everything else is 'aes setup's job. The bootstrapper
must never grow a second responsibility.

THE ARCH TRAP (this is the one that bites): 'uname -m' returns x86_64/aarch64
on some systems, while the release assets and Go use amd64/arm64. install.sh
must translate ONCE, before constructing the URL:
    x86_64  -> amd64
    aarch64 -> arm64
A silent fallback is forbidden -- if the mapping is unknown, error out.

RELEASE ASSET NAMING (fixed so install.sh needs no manifest):
    aes-<version>-<goos>-<goarch>.tar.gz
    checksums.txt            (sha256sum format, covers every asset)

The Go binary is fully self-contained: no Go, brew, or apt required on the
target machine. That is the whole point of a prebuilt binary.

SECURITY:
- checksum is MANDATORY and verified BEFORE extraction
- a mismatch aborts; the binary is NOT placed
- validate the tarball does not contain path traversal entries before
  extracting

scripts/build.sh cross-compiles darwin/{arm64,amd64} + linux/{amd64,arm64}.
release.yml runs the build matrix, attaches checksums.txt, publishes on tag.

Tests (shell-level, no root):
- correct asset + matching checksum -> binary placed and runs
- CHECKSUM MISMATCH -> abort, binary NOT placed (the absence is the contract)
- unknown OS/arch -> clear error, no junk download attempted
- a local file:// or fixture server serves a test tarball; install.sh is
  parameterised to take a base URL so tests do not hit the network
- tarball with a ../ entry -> rejected

Done when: on a clean Ubuntu box, 'curl ... | sh' yields a working
'aes --version'.
close_reason: Stage 0 landed: install.sh (5 steps only, uname->Go arch translated once, mandatory sha256 before extraction, path-traversal rejection, base-URL param for offline tests), scripts/build.sh (4-target cross-compile, CGO off, checksums.txt), .github/workflows/release.yml, cmd/aes/main.go, Makefile. 9 shell assertions green over file:// fixture; all 4 targets verified correct platform + statically linked.

title: Profile format + profile loader with require_tested gate
description:
Package: internal/profile

Format (locked in spec):
  # profiles/default.yaml
  name: default
  description: Verified AI coding environment
  include:
    - ripgrep        # explicit tools
  tags:              # or whole categories
    - search
    - git
  require_tested: true   # I15

resolve_tested gate: when require_tested is true, ANY resolved tool with
tested:false fails validation with an error NAMING THE TOOL. This is what
makes the North Star honest -- 'complete, VERIFIED environment' is a lie if
untested tools are in the default profile, and 25 never-run tools are exactly
where it breaks on a user's first machine.

Ship these profiles:
  minimal   -- git, ripgrep, jq. The floor.
  developer -- minimal + build tools, language runtimes
  ai        -- developer + coding agents (claude, codex, opencode)
  full      -- everything with tested:true
default.yaml is an alias for 'ai' given the tool's positioning.

Tests:
- a profile with require_tested:true referencing an untested tool -> error
  NAMING that tool
- require_tested:false with untested tools -> loads fine
- include by name -> resolves that tool
- tags by category -> resolves all tools in those categories
- a referenced tool that does not exist -> error naming it (never silently
  resolve to an empty set -- a typo'd profile that installs nothing is the
  worst possible failure for a 'setup' command)
- unknown profile name -> error listing valid profiles
- profiles/ dir missing a file -> error, not a silent empty profile

Depends on manifest, catalog.
close_reason: internal/profile landed: profile loader with require_tested gate (I15) naming every offender, selectors matching both tags and categories, unknown name/tag always an error (never a silent empty selection), deterministic dedup+sort. Shipped profiles/{minimal,developer,ai,full,default}.yaml all require_tested:true. 3 mutations (gate, unknown-name, empty-selector) all caught.

title: Test layer 1: verify fixtures on real tools
description:
Runs on every 'go test'. No mutation.

Eight tools already present on the dev machine. Install is SKIPPED; verify is
the assertion:
  ripgrep/rg, git/git, fzf/fzf, jq/jq, tmux/tmux, zoxide/zoxide, gh/gh,
  claude/claude

A tool marked tested:true in the catalog that FAILS this fixture must be
flipped to tested:false. The test and the catalog flag are coupled -- if the
fixture fails, the flag is wrong.

CRITICAL ANTI-PATTERN: the test must assert against a GOOS-derived
expectation, NEVER the host's actual identity. A test that reads
runtime.GOOS and then compares against runtime.GOOS passes on the dev
machine and fails on every other developer's box, or worse, passes
everywhere while checking nothing. Either skip when the tool is absent, or
assert a property that holds regardless of host.

These are tagged with a build tag or a -short skip so the suite still runs on
a machine that lacks some of them, but the tool's 'tested' flag reflects what
was actually verified on THIS machine.

Done when: 'go test ./...' is green on the dev machine and asserts something
real about each of the eight tools.

All 16 cases pass on this machine. Found+fixed a version-parser fidelity issue: tmux ships 3.6b, digits-only regex reported 3.6; now reports 3.6b with leadingInt so the comparison tolerates the suffix. Mutation-verified: reverting leadingInt makes Layer 1 fail on the real tmux with Status=stale.

title: Real tool catalog: 40-50 definitions, 10-15 marked tested
description:
Files: tools/<category>/<name>/tool.yaml, 40-50 total

LAYOUT: category is a DIRECTORY for human organisation, but Category is a
FIELD and is the source of truth. Never infer the category from the path --
moving a file must not change its meaning.

SPLIT:
  10-15 tools  tested:true   -- passed BOTH test layers
  25-35 tools  tested:false  -- valid definitions, NOT in the default profile
                               (I15). This is the expansion pool.

CATEGORIES: shell, search, terminal, git, runtime, ai, agent, infra, utility

CONTENT PRIORITY -- cover the ACFS ecosystem, not just generic dev tools.
This positioning is 'Agent Developer Environment Manager', so the ai/ and
agent/ categories carry the identity:
  ai:      claude, codex, opencode, gemini
  agent:   beads, ntm, cass, ubs, dcg, agent-mail
  shell:   zsh, bash, starship
  search:  ripgrep, fd, fzf
  terminal: tmux, btop, eza, bat, dust
  git:     git, gh, git-lfs, delta, lazygit
  runtime: go, node, python, rust, mise
  infra:   docker, kubectl, terraform, vault
  utility: jq, yq, httpie, direnv, tree, ncdu

EVERY definition needs BOTH a darwin and a linux install target unless the
tool is genuinely single-platform (and then a comment says why). Prefer
github-release with a pinned version + sha256 over a package manager: it is
independent of the package manager, needs no sudo, and has an explicit
checksum. Use package(brew/apt) only when no release exists or when the tool
is a system library.

Every tool needs a verify block. verify.version.min must be parseable as
\d+(\.\d+)*.

Tests:
- every file in tools/ passes manifest validation (a test that walks the tree
  and validates each -- so a typo'd tool.yaml fails CI, not setup)
- every dependency name referenced actually exists in the catalog
- no dependency cycles across the whole catalog
- every tool with tested:true is in the Layer-1 fixture set
- every tool has install targets for both darwin and linux, or a documented
  single-platform exception
- 'aes list' shows the whole catalog with correct statuses

Depends on manifest, catalog, profile, verifier.

title: Test layer 2 + sandbox: prove the real install path
description:
Layer 1 proves DETECTION. It does NOT prove the install path -- a manifest
can verify a tool perfectly and still install the wrong thing, or nothing.
Only a real install proves that. This bead is where that gets proven.

Files: internal/sandbox/ (or scripts/sandbox/), plus the aes test command.

SANDBOX: Ubuntu 24.04 container via Docker. Real apt, real binaries, real
verification, real PATH, real shell. The host's ~/.aes is NOT touched --
the sandbox gets its own AES_HOME so the two never interfere.
macOS: a container cannot faithfully model Homebrew or macOS semantics, so
macOS uses host-safe mode (real install of a github-release tool into a
temp AES_HOME) plus an optional VM for the full path.

PER-TOOL SEQUENCE, from a machine where the tool is ABSENT:
  1. aes setup --only <tool> --yes        -> must exit 0
  2. the binary exists, Verify -> StatusOK
  3. state.json contains the entry
  4. re-run aes setup --only <tool> --yes -> idempotent, installer NOT called
  5. delete the binary, run aes doctor     -> DRIFT detected
  6. re-run aes setup --only <tool> --force -> reinstalls

Steps 4-6 are the ones that catch real bugs:
  - a non-idempotent installer
  - a state writer that records something the installer never did
  - a doctor that cannot see drift

A tool may be marked tested:true ONLY when BOTH layers pass. 'tested' means
both, not just Layer 1.

Tests:
- the sandbox harness itself: create, run, clean up
- the host AES_HOME is byte-identical before and after a sandbox run
- --keep-sandbox leaves the directory for debugging
- a deliberately broken tool.yaml in the sandbox produces exit 3 and installs
  nothing (proves the failure path, not just the happy path)
- the full 7-step sequence for at least 3 tools spanning 3 different
  strategies (github-release, brew, apt)

Depends on setup, installer, verifier, state, doctor.

title: TUI: same core, three hard constraints
description:
Command: bare 'aes'. Menu: Setup, Tools, Profiles, Doctor, Environment.

Tools screen: search/filter, tick to select several, Enter -> the SAME
resolver, the SAME installer, the SAME verify. Selecting rust pulls in cargo
automatically. This is 'aes setup --only rust' with a different selection UI.

THREE HARD CONSTRAINTS -- these are what keep the TUI from rotting into a
second implementation:

 1. NO free-form command entry. The TUI must never accept 'brew install xxx'.
    Breaks I1/I3; the YAML is data, do not reopen a shell.
 2. NO fast path that bypasses the resolver. TUI and CLI must produce the
    SAME Actions or I13 is violated and the two frontends diverge.
 3. NO install business logic inside the TUI. Every decision belongs to core.

The TUI does exactly this: collect selection -> call the core -> display
results. Like ssh, which does not configure its own port forwarding.

KEYBINDINGS (locked):
  up/down    navigate
  space      toggle selection
  /          search/filter
  enter      install selection
  esc        back / clear search
  q          quit

Tests:
- the Tools screen's Request is byte-identical to what
  'aes setup --only <selection>' would produce (I13)
- no code path in the TUI package reaches the installer directly
- a static check (or a code-review-enforced constraint) that internal/tui
  does not import internal/installer
- quitting mid-selection does not mutate anything
- an empty selection Enter is a no-op, not an error

Depends on setup, cli, resolver. NOTE: bare 'aes' currently prints help;
this bead replaces that with the TUI.

title: Publish: GitHub repo, CI matrix, README, releases
description:
FINAL bead. Do this only after every other bead is closed and the DoD is met.

 1. Create the public GitHub repository and push.
 2. README: North Star, the two frontends (agent aes setup / human aes), the
    install path (curl | sh), the 15 invariants, and the --dry-run /
    doctor workflow. Lead with what the user gets, not with the architecture.
 3. CI matrix: build + test on macOS (arm64) and Ubuntu (amd64). The test
    suite must pass on BOTH -- that is the cross-platform promise, and it is
    the only automated guard against a Linux-only regression.
 4. Release workflow: on tag -> cross-compile all four platforms, attach
    binaries + checksums.txt (the contract install.sh depends on).
 5. LICENSE. Pick deliberately and state it in the README.
 6. Verify the whole loop from a genuinely clean environment:
       curl ... | sh  ->  aes --version  ->  aes setup --dry-run
    Do not assume; actually run it. A broken bootstrap is the one failure
    that makes the tool unusable for everyone.

Definition of Done, all must be checked:
  - 15 invariants covered by tests
  - 10 MVP assertions green
  - 40-50 tool definitions, >=10 tested:true (both layers)
  - aes setup bootstraps end to end in one command, exit 0 only after verify
  - ~/.aes is the only boundary; ~/.agents is never touched
  - TUI == CLI (identical Actions)
  - sandbox proves it works on real Ubuntu

Do not publish while the DoD has unchecked boxes. A half-working tool with
a public URL is worse than no URL.

title: Language-ecosystem installers: go, npm, cargo, uv
description:
Packages: internal/installer/{go,npm,cargo,uv}.go

The manifest schema declares five strategies; four are implemented by other
beads (github-release, package/brew, package/apt). These are the remaining
three, plus uv.

Each is a thin adapter over an ecosystem's own installer, NOT a
reimplementation of it. aes decides WHICH package and WHETHER it is already
present; the ecosystem tool decides how to fetch and link.

  go:     go install <go_package>@<version>   -> writes to ~/go/bin
  npm:    npm install -g <npm_package>@<ver> -> writes to the user prefix
  cargo:  cargo install <cargo_name>         -> writes to ~/.cargo/bin
  uv:     uv tool install <package>          -> writes to ~/.local/bin

GATING: each of these REQUIRES its base toolchain. If 'go' is not on PATH,
the go-strategy installer must NOT attempt 'go install' -- it should report
that the toolchain is missing and name it, so the catalog can declare the
toolchain itself as a dependency. That is what the dependency DAG is for;
the installer does not go looking for a toolchain.

NO PRIVILEGE: none of these four need sudo. All write to user-owned
directories. RequiresPrivilege is false for all -- a fact that must be
asserted, not assumed.

VERSION PINNING: prefer an explicit version over @latest. An unpinned
ecosystem install is the same supply-chain risk as an unpinned GitHub
release.

Tests (with an injected fake runner -- do NOT actually install anything):
- missing toolchain -> clear error naming the required toolchain, no run
- present toolchain -> runner called with the exact expected command line
- RequiresPrivilege is false for all four (assert the derived value)
- the destination directory is reported so envgen can add it to PATH
- a pinned version is included in the command; an absent version is REJECTED
  at validation time rather than defaulting to @latest at runtime
- npm without a writable global prefix -> error surfaces the actual npm
  message rather than swallowing it

Depends on manifest, exec, installer registry. Feeds envgen (destination
paths become PATH entries).
close_reason: Language-ecosystem installers landed: shared Ecosystem adapter + go/npm/cargo/uv constructors, toolchain gate (missing toolchain errors, never runs, never hunts), Destination() seam for envgen PATH, all four privilege-free (asserted), pinned @version coordinates enforced at manifest load. 59 installer assertions; toolchain gate and privilege derivation both mutation-verified.

title: uninstall and forget: honest lifecycle commands
description:
Stage 10. Two commands with STRICTLY different meanings -- a command called
'remove' that only drops a state entry is a lie about what it did, and the
whole point of AES is that its commands say what they do.

aes uninstall <tool>
  Invokes the strategy's real removal:
    github-release -> delete the binary from ~/.aes/bin
    package/brew   -> brew uninstall <package>
    package/apt    -> sudo apt remove, under the SAME privilege model
                      (print, confirm / sudo -n, exit 5)
    go/npm/cargo/uv -> REPORTED AS NOT REMOVED, with the reason. These
                      ecosystems do not offer clean per-package removal;
                      pretending otherwise leaves the user with a broken
                      install they did not ask for.
  Then removes the state entry ONLY after verify confirms the binary is gone.
  If the binary survives the uninstall, the state entry STAYS and doctor
  reports the disagreement. Removing state for a tool that is still on disk
  is how drift gets created in the first place.

aes forget <tool>
  Drops the state entry only. The binary stays exactly where it is. This is
  the correct command for a tool aes did not install -- one you had before
  installing aes, which is the common case for a developer machine.
  Use it when doctor reports 'unmanaged' and you want aes to stop thinking
  about that tool.

BOTH must refuse to touch a tool that is not in state (nothing to do), and
both must confirm before acting unless --yes is passed.

Tests:
- uninstall of a github-release tool -> binary gone, state entry gone
- uninstall where the binary survives -> state entry RETAINED, exit 6
- uninstall of a go-strategy tool -> reports not-removed with a reason,
  does NOT silently pretend success
- uninstall of an apt-strategy tool -> privilege model respected, no silent
  sudo
- uninstall of a tool absent from state -> no-op, clear message
- forget -> state entry gone, binary STILL PRESENT (assert the file exists)
- forget on an unmanaged tool -> succeeds
- neither command ever runs without confirmation unless --yes
- uninstall does not remove DEPENDENTS automatically; it lists tools that
  depend on the one being removed and asks

Depends on installer, verifier, state, cli.
